title: Review where the risk is
glance: Neither review everything nor review nothing: approval before irreversible or high-impact actions, automation plus random audits for low-risk volume, and full review only when every output carries real weight.
story: Human-in-the-loop means a person checks or approves some of what an AI system does. The two easy answers are both traps. Reviewing everything sounds safe, but at high volume reviewers start rubber-stamping (approving without really checking), so the control stops working while the cost stays. Reviewing nothing leaves the rare expensive mistake unguarded.

The fix is to place people by risk. Actions that cannot be undone or carry high value need a person's approval before they happen, because an audit afterwards cannot reverse the harm. Low-value, reversible, high-volume work runs automatically, and a random sample is audited to measure the true error rate. Routing rules, such as an amount threshold, are enforced in code, not left to the model's own sense of confidence, which can be high even when it is wrong.

Sometimes the strict answer is right: when every output carries legal or safety weight, every one is reviewed. And review works better when reviewers see the evidence next to the summary, and when their corrections are kept as data to improve the system.
situation: A hospital supply agent reorders stock by placing purchase orders with approved suppliers, about 2,000 a week. Most are routine consumables under $500. A few each week are for equipment over $50,000, and an order cannot be cancelled once the supplier ships. Leadership wants as much automation as is safe. Which review design fits best?

options.t: Place every order automatically, and have staff audit a random sample each week.
Have a buyer approve every order before it is placed with the supplier.
A buyer approves orders above a set value before they are placed; the rest go automatically.
Hold an order for a buyer only when the agent rates its own confidence as low.

worlds.name: As written
worlds.fact: Most orders are small, but a few each week are over $50,000 and cannot be cancelled once shipped.
worlds.why: A value threshold, enforced in code, puts a buyer in front of the rare irreversible, high-value orders and lets the routine volume run automatically.

losers.A: An audit finds a wrong $50,000 order after it has shipped, when it can no longer be cancelled.
losers.B: Buyers would approve 2,000 orders a week, mostly trivial ones, and would soon rubber-stamp them, including the large ones.
losers.D: The agent can be confidently wrong, so a large wrong order could go through without anyone seeing it.

worlds.name: Every order carries legal weight
worlds.fact: The agent now reorders only controlled drugs. Every order must match the hospital's licence, and any wrong order is a reportable legal breach.
worlds.why: When every output carries legal weight, every one needs a person's approval before it happens. Here the cost of full review is justified.

losers.A: An audit after the fact finds a breach that has already happened.
losers.C: A value threshold assumes small orders are low risk; here a small wrong order is still a legal breach.
losers.D: Self-rated confidence is a weak signal, and a confidently wrong controlled-drug order is still a breach.

worlds.name: Everything is small and reversible
worlds.fact: Equipment is now bought separately. Every order the agent places is a consumable under $500, and any order can be cancelled free of charge until it ships the next day.
worlds.why: Low value, reversible and high volume: automate, and audit a random sample to measure the real error rate and catch drift.

losers.B: Approving 2,000 small, cancellable orders a week costs a lot of buyer time and invites rubber-stamping, for little risk.
losers.C: No order ever crosses the threshold, so the approval tier does nothing, and without a sample audit nobody measures the error rate.
losers.D: Confidence-based holds are unreliable and give no measure of how many automatic orders are wrong.

signals: “high volume, mostly correct, easy to reverse”
“regulation requires a qualified person to sign each one”
remember: Put people where an error is costly and cannot be undone, before the action. Automate the low-risk volume and audit a random sample. Route on rules in code, not the model's own confidence.

practice.stem: An airline's maintenance assistant drafts the records that release an aircraft back into service after repairs. Aviation rules require a licensed engineer to certify each release, and a wrong record could let an unsafe aircraft fly. The airline wants to cut the engineers' paperwork time. Which review design fits best?
options: Engineers audit a random sample of the records released, at the end of every week.
Engineers review only the drafts that the assistant itself marks as uncertain.
An engineer checks and certifies every draft, with the evidence shown beside it.
Records for minor repairs release automatically; major ones go to an engineer.
practice.why: The deciding fact: every record carries safety and legal weight, and the rules require certification of each one. The saving comes from showing evidence, not from skipping review.
traps: Works for low-risk volume, but an unsafe aircraft could fly before the audit.
Works poorly anywhere; the assistant can be confidently wrong, and rules require every record certified.
Works when small items are low risk, but every release here needs a licensed engineer.

practice.stem: A bank's loan-modification assistant prepares cases that an officer must approve, because each decision changes a customer's repayments. Officers spend about twenty minutes per case searching the customer's documents for the figures behind the assistant's summary, and the backlog is growing. What should the architect change?
options: Let the assistant approve cases it rates as high confidence, and send the rest to officers.
Approve cases automatically and have officers audit a random sample each week.
Add more officers to the team until the backlog falls to an acceptable level.
Show each figure in the summary next to the passage of the document it came from.
practice.why: The deciding fact: every case still needs an officer, and the time goes into finding the evidence. Putting the evidence beside the summary makes each review faster and better.
traps: Works poorly; confidence is a weak signal, and these decisions need an officer's approval.
Works for low-impact volume, but each decision changes a customer's repayments.
Works to clear the queue, but it pays for the same slow search on every case.

practice.stem: An insurer's claims assistant drafts letters that handlers review before sending. Handlers correct about 8% of drafts in the review tool, but the corrections are discarded. Next quarter, leadership wants to stop reviewing the claim categories that are safe to automate. What should the architect put in place now?
options: A monthly survey asking handlers how far they now trust the assistant's drafts.
Keep each correction with its category, and measure error rates per category.
Stop reviewing the claim category that draws the fewest customer complaints.
A second model that checks every draft, so that handlers can be removed.
practice.why: The deciding fact: the corrections already exist and show where errors happen. Keeping them by category gives the evidence to decide where review can safely stop.
traps: Works to gauge morale, but trust is self-reported, not a measured error rate.
Works as a hint, but few complaints can mean errors go unnoticed, not that none happen.
Works as an extra check, but it removes people before anyone knows the error rates.
